causal_agent: Tomato yellow leaf curl virus (TYLCV), genus Begomovirus, family Geminiviridae
distribution: Worldwide, especially tropical and subtropical regions

vector.species: Bemisia tabaci (silverleaf or sweet potato whitefly)
notes: Females transmit virus more efficiently than males
Transovarial transmission observed for two generations

symptoms.overall_impact: Yield losses of 90–100% possible in severe outbreaks

disease_cycle: Virus introduced via infected seedlings, contaminated tools, or whitefly vector
Once established, whiteflies spread virus rapidly from plant to plant
Virus persists in alternative hosts including weeds and other solanaceous crops
Environmental factors such as warm tropical climates favor virus proliferation

cultural: Plant TYLCV-resistant or tolerant tomato varieties
Rotate crops to non-hosts to reduce inoculum
Use greenhouse production to reduce vector access
chemical: Apply insecticides targeting Bemisia tabaci, rotating or mixing active ingredients to prevent resistance
Timing of applications is critical due to rapid virus transmission by whiteflies
genetic: Breeding or transgenic approaches to produce TYLCV-resistant tomato lines

notes: TYLCV is one of the most serious viral diseases of tomato globally
Developing countries are most affected due to climate and high cost of control measures
Integrated pest management combining resistant varieties, vector control, and cultural practices is most effective
references: Czosnek, H. & Laterrot, H. 1997. Tomato yellow leaf curl virus, an emerging virus complex causing epidemics worldwide. Adv Virus Res 47: 85–138.
Polston, J.E. & Lapidot, M. 2007. Management of Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus: A review. Plant Dis 91: 125–134.
Brown, J.K., 2015. The Bemisia tabaci species complex and TYLCV transmission. Virus Res 202: 150–162.
